decks.c: SE401: Introduction — Introduction to Software Testing
n: Why is testing necessary? Testing reduces the risk of failures in operation (Ariane 5, Therac-25, failed satellites, bank errors): poor quality is very expensive.
Ariane 5 (1996): reused Ariane 4 code overflowed converting a 64-bit float to a 16-bit integer: not a coding slip, an untested assumption.
Assessment A Self Test
Software Testing Terminologies

A human makes an ERROR (mistake) → it leaves a DEFECT (fault, bug) in the code → running it may cause a FAILURE (wrong observable behaviour). Tip A human makes an ERROR (mistake) → it leaves a DEFECT (fault, bug) in the code → running it may cause a FAILURE (wrong observable behaviour).
Verdicts: pass, fail, inconclusive.
Test oracle: the mechanism that decides whether an output is correct (expected results, a reference implementation, assertions).
Fixture: the fixed state the tests run against. Suite: a collection of test cases. Scaffolding: drivers, stubs, harnesses.

The seven test principles Seven principles: testing shows presence of defects (not absence) · exhaustive testing is impossible · early testing · defect clustering · pesticide paradox · testing is context dependent · absence-of-errors fallacy. Tip Seven principles: testing shows presence of defects (not absence) · exhaustive testing is impossible · early testing · defect clustering · pesticide paradox · testing is context dependent · absence-of-errors fallacy.
Testing can show defects are present, never that they are absent.
Exhaustive testing is impossible except in trivial cases: use risk and priorities.
Defect clustering: a small number of modules contain most of the defects (Pareto).
Pesticide paradox: repeating the same tests finds no new bugs: review and add tests regularly.
Absence-of-errors fallacy: a bug-free system that doesn’t meet users’ needs is still a failure.
Fundamental Test Processes Fundamental test process: planning and control → analysis and design → implementation and execution → evaluating exit criteria and reporting → test closure.
The psychology of testing Psychology: testers need curiosity, professional pessimism, attention to detail, good communication; report defects objectively.
Independence levels: the author tests their own code → another developer → an independent test team → outside organization. More independence finds different defects.
Limitations of Software Testing
"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence." (Dijkstra)

decks.t: Testing throughout the SDLC — Testing throughout the Software Development Life Cycle
decks.c: SE401: Testing throughout the SDLC — Testing throughout the Software Development Life Cycle
n: Verification: "Are we building the product RIGHT?" (meets its specification). Validation: "Are we building the RIGHT product?" (meets users’ needs). Tip Verification: "Are we building the product RIGHT?" (meets its specification). Validation: "Are we building the RIGHT product?" (meets users’ needs).
V-model: each development phase on the left has a matching test level on the right (requirements ↔ acceptance, design ↔ system/integration, code ↔ component).
Testing should begin as early as possible: reviews of requirements and designs find defects when they are cheapest.
Component (unit) testing: individual components in isolation, usually by developers, often with stubs and drivers.
Integration testing: interfaces and interactions between components (component integration) or systems (system integration).
System testing: the behaviour of the whole system against the requirements, in an environment close to production.
Acceptance testing: establish confidence that the system is fit for use: user acceptance, operational, contract and regulation, alpha and beta.
Functional testing: WHAT the system does. Non-functional: HOW WELL (performance, load, usability, security, reliability).

Confirmation testing (re-testing): check that a fixed defect is really fixed. Regression testing: check that the change broke nothing else. Exam trap Re-testing confirms the FIX; regression testing looks for SIDE EFFECTS.
Maintenance testing: triggered by modifications, migration or retirement of a live system; includes impact analysis and regression testing.
No slides match this filter.
Chaos report: only a minority of projects succeed (on time, on budget, full scope); the rest are challenged or fail.
HealthCare.gov (2013): ~$500M+, crashed at launch: changing requirements, late and inadequate testing (no end-to-end test until days before launch), poor management.
MTTF: mean time to failure. MTTR: mean time to repair. MTBF = MTTF + MTTR.
Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) × 100%.
"Five nines" (99.999%) availability ≈ 5 minutes of downtime a year.
Qualities: correctness, reliability, robustness, safety, performance, usability, security, maintainability, reusability, portability, interoperability.
Correctness: consistent with the specification (all or nothing). Reliability: probability of operating without failure under a usage profile (statistical).
Safety: prevents undesirable behaviours (hazards). Robustness: behaves reasonably (degrades gracefully) outside normal conditions.
Cost of quality: prevention (training, reviews) + appraisal (testing) + internal failure (rework before release) + external failure (after release: support, recalls).
The later a defect is found, the more it costs to fix (up to 100× after release).
Verification: does it meet the specification? Validation: does it meet the user’s real needs? Seen again ↻ Testing throughout the SDLC, slide 4 · V&V
V-model: user requirements ↔ acceptance test, system spec ↔ system test, design ↔ integration test, code ↔ unit test.
Alpha testing: by potential users at the developer’s site (controlled). Beta: by real users in their own environment.

decks.t: Quality — Quality Assurance, Quality Control and Metrics
decks.c: SE401: Quality — Quality Assurance, Quality Control and Metrics
n: Software Quality
Quality Assurance Quality assurance (QA): PROCESS-oriented, preventive: make sure the right processes are followed so defects aren’t introduced.
Quality Control Quality control (QC): PRODUCT-oriented, detective: inspect and test the product to find defects. Memory trick QA = prevent (process). QC = detect (product). Testing is part of QC.
Project Success
Success factors: executive support, user involvement, experienced project manager, clear objectives, small scope, standard infrastructure.
Measurement and Metrics
Measure: a quantitative value of an attribute. Metric: a measure related to a goal (defects per KLOC).
Product metrics (size, complexity, defects), process metrics (effort, defect-removal efficiency), project metrics (cost, schedule).
Direct measures: LOC, execution speed, defects. Indirect: functionality, quality, complexity, maintainability.
Size-oriented metrics normalise by size: errors per KLOC, cost per KLOC, pages of documentation per KLOC. No slides match this filter.
Test selection
Test case: inputs, preconditions, expected results and postconditions for one test objective. Must be repeatable.
Good test cases: simple, one thing at a time, traceable to requirements, with a clear expected result.
Triangle problem: classify three sides as equilateral, isosceles, scalene, or not a triangle: include invalid inputs (0, negatives, a + b ≤ c).
Testing is "complete" when exit criteria are met (coverage, remaining risk, time/budget), never when all bugs are gone.
Test driver: code that CALLS the unit under test. Stub: replaces a module the unit calls. Harness: drivers + stubs + tools. Seen again ↻ Unit Testing and JUnit, slide 4 · unit testing
Oracle: decides pass/fail (comparison-based with expected outputs, or checks of properties).
Smoke test: a quick subset of tests to check the build is stable enough for further testing.

decks.t: Test Design Techniques — Test Design Techniques
decks.c: SE401: Test Design Techniques — Test Design Techniques
n: Test development: test analysis (what to test: test conditions) → test design (how: test cases) → test implementation (procedures, scripts, schedule).
Case Study – Knight Capital High Frequency Trading (HFT) Knight Capital (2012): dead "zombie" code reactivated during a deployment lost $440M in 45 minutes: missing regression and deployment testing.
Black-box (specification-based) vs. white-box (structure-based) vs. experience-based techniques.
Equivalence partitioning: divide inputs into classes expected to behave the same; one test per class (valid and invalid).
Boundary value analysis: errors cluster at edges: test min, max and just outside/inside them.
Decision tables: combinations of conditions → actions; each rule (column) is a test case; collapse rules whose outcome doesn’t depend on a condition.
State transition testing: states, events, transitions and actions; cover every valid transition and try invalid (null) ones.
Use-case testing: one test per main and alternative flow; good for acceptance and system tests.
General Testing
Non-functional: performance (response time), load (expected volume), stress (beyond the limits), security, usability, recovery, compatibility.
Error guessing: use experience to anticipate likely mistakes (empty inputs, zero, nulls).
Exploratory testing: simultaneous learning, test design and execution, often time-boxed.

decks.c: SE401: White Box Testing — White-Box Testing
n: White-box (structural) testing needs access to the code; tests are derived from its structure.
Static testing: examine code without running it (reviews, walkthroughs, inspections, static analysis).
Formal inspection: author, moderator, reader, recorder/scribe, inspectors; preparation, meeting, rework, follow-up.
Coverage criteria from weak to strong: statement → branch/decision → condition → decision/condition → multiple-condition → path.

Statement coverage: every statement executed at least once. Weak: can miss the false branch of an if. Exam trap 100% statement coverage does NOT imply 100% branch coverage; 100% branch coverage DOES imply 100% statement coverage.
Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2 = decision nodes + 1 = number of independent paths (minimum tests for basis path coverage).
Case (i): A hypothetical program with no decision node

Case (i): A hypothetical program with no decision node # of independent paths = 1 # of nodes, N = 2; # of edges, E = 1; Cyclomatic complexity = E – N + 2 = 1 # of predicate nodes, P = 0; Cyclomatic complexity = P + 1 = 1 End
Decision (branch) coverage: every decision takes both true and false outcomes.
Condition coverage: every individual condition in a decision takes both true and false. Doesn’t guarantee decision coverage.
Decision/condition coverage: both every condition AND every decision take both outcomes.
No slides match this filter.
Code coverage: the percentage of code (statements, branches, functions, lines) executed by the test suite.
Coverage finds UNTESTED code; it does not prove the tested code is correct: high coverage can give a false sense of security.
Benefit: pinpoints which files and branches lack tests, guiding where to write more.
Coverage ≠ quality-tested code; a coverage target must not replace code review.
Write tests from the specification first, then use coverage to see what you missed.
Google guideline: 60% acceptable, 75% commendable, 90% exemplary (no single "ideal" number).
Make sure frequently changing code is covered (per-commit coverage goals).
Gate deployments on coverage carefully: thresholds can become a checkbox that encourages bad tests.

decks.t: Unit Testing and JUnit — Unit Testing and JUnit
decks.c: SE401: Unit Testing and JUnit — Unit Testing and JUnit
n: Unit Testing and JUnit
Unit testing: test one unit (method/class) in isolation, written by developers, run automatically and often.
JUnit: a framework for writing repeatable automated Java tests; a test method is annotated @Test and returns void.
An Introduction to JUnit Part 1: The Basics
Verdicts: pass, fail (assertion failed), error (unexpected exception).
Assertions: Boolean checks that make the test fail if they are false.
Assertion Methods

assertEquals(expected, actual), assertTrue, assertFalse, assertNull, assertNotNull, assertSame (same reference), assertArrayEquals. Exam trap assertEquals uses equals(); assertSame checks the two references are the SAME object.
Floating point: assertEquals(expected, actual, delta), e.g. assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 0.0001).
Expected exceptions: assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> obj.method(-1));
JUnit Best Practices
Each test must be independent of the others (no shared mutable state, any order).
@BeforeEach / @AfterEach run before/after EVERY test; @BeforeAll / @AfterAll run once per class and must be static.
@RepeatedTest(n) runs a test n times.
No slides match this filter.
Changes (fixes, new features, refactoring, new environments) can break unchanged parts, uncover old bugs or reintroduce fixed ones.
Regression test: re-test a previously tested program after modification to make sure no new defects were introduced in unchanged areas.
Keep a test suite, run it after every change, compare with previous results, add new tests as needed.
Problems: maintaining the test suite, and the cost of re-testing (proportional to product size, not change size).
Obsolete test: no longer valid for the changed system. Redundant test: doesn’t differ significantly from others.
Selection: run only the tests relevant to the change. Prioritization: run the most important ones first when time is short.
Code-based selection: only tests that execute changed or new code.
Prioritized rotating selection: run all tests eventually, some sooner (round robin, track record of finding faults, structural coverage).

decks.t: Testing Metrics and Tools — Testing Metrics and Tools
decks.c: SE401: Testing Metrics and Tools — Testing Metrics and Tools
n: "You cannot improve what you cannot measure": metrics show progress, quality and where to act.
Base metrics: raw counts (test cases written, executed, passed, failed, blocked; defects found). Calculated metrics are derived from them.
Examples: % test cases executed = executed / total × 100; pass rate = passed / executed × 100; defect density = defects / size (KLOC).
Defect removal efficiency (DRE) = defects found before release / (before + after release) × 100.
Testing Tools
Tools support test management, static testing, test design, execution and logging, performance and monitoring.
Static analysis tools (SpotBugs, checkstyle, JDepend) find defects in code without running it.
Test execution tools run scripted tests; harnesses and unit frameworks provide drivers and stubs.
Benefits: less repetitive work, consistency, objective assessment. Risks: unrealistic expectations, underestimated effort, over-reliance on the tool.
Interview Questions and Answers
Stop testing when exit criteria are met: coverage, defect rates, deadlines, budget, acceptable residual risk.
No slides match this filter.
Web Testing
Website: mostly static informational pages. Web application: interactive client–server program run in a browser.
Web testing: functionality, usability, interface, compatibility, security, performance.
Functionality: check all links (broken, internal, external, mailto), forms, cookies, HTML/CSS validity, database integrity.
Compatibility: browsers, operating systems, devices, screen sizes.
Security: unauthorized access, session expiry, SQL injection, XSS, HTTPS.
Performance: load and stress testing of the site.
Selenium: open-source tool to automate browser testing.
Mobile Testing
Native apps (built for one platform), mobile web apps (run in the browser), hybrid apps (web code inside a native wrapper).
Mobile challenges: many devices and OS versions, screen sizes, networks, battery, interruptions (calls, notifications).
Also test installation, interruptions, crash recovery and battery/network conditions.
